Q: How do scalars, vectors, matrices and tensors describe model data?
A: A scalar is one value; a vector has one indexed axis; a matrix has two; a tensor generalizes this to more axes. Shape specifies axis lengths but not their meaning. An image tensor might represent batch, channel, height and width, while a text tensor uses batch, position and feature axes. A shape-compatible operation can still be semantically wrong if axes are swapped. Write axis meanings and units alongside dimensions before multiplying or broadcasting arrays.
Why: A matrix of 32 examples by 10 features multiplied by 10 features by 3 outputs produces 32 by 3 predictions. Swapping the example and feature axes changes the intended operation even if another compatible matrix happens to make it run.
Risk: Broadcasting can hide a misplaced axis by producing a plausible but incorrect shape.
Trade: Explicit shapes improve review and debugging at little runtime cost.
Try: Annotate each axis and derive the output shape of a batched linear layer.
worked_case: A matrix of 32 examples by 10 features multiplied by 10 features by 3 outputs produces 32 by 3 predictions. Swapping the example and feature axes changes the intended operation even if another compatible matrix happens to make it run.

Q: What do a dot product, matrix multiplication and vector norm measure?
A: A dot product sums products of aligned coordinates and depends on both magnitude and direction. Matrix multiplication applies these weighted combinations to rows and columns. A norm measures size under its chosen definition; the Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both norms, removing magnitude for nonzero vectors. These operations acquire meaning from the representation and task, not from the formula alone. A zero vector requires an explicit cosine policy.
Why: Vectors [2,0] and [1,0] have dot product 2 and cosine 1. A larger dot product does not mean a higher probability, and rescaling an unnormalized representation can change rankings.
Risk: Normalization can discard a magnitude signal the model intentionally learned.
Trade: Follow the representation's metric contract and evaluate task outcomes.
Try: Calculate dot product, lengths and cosine for two nonzero vectors and one zero-vector edge case.
worked_case: Vectors [2,0] and [1,0] have dot product 2 and cosine 1. A larger dot product does not mean a higher probability, and rescaling an unnormalized representation can change rankings.

Q: How do eigenvectors, SVD and PCA connect to dimensionality reduction?
A: An eigenvector keeps its direction under a square linear transformation, scaled by an eigenvalue. Singular value decomposition factors a matrix into orthogonal input/output directions and nonnegative singular values. Principal component analysis uses high-variance directions of centered data to build a lower-dimensional representation. Fit centering and component selection using training data only. High variance does not guarantee target relevance, fairness or preserved rare signals, so assess downstream performance rather than treating explained variance as the final quality metric.
Why: A rare fraud signal can contribute little overall variance and disappear when only the largest components are retained. A high explained-variance percentage can therefore coexist with worse detection of the important minority case.
Risk: Fitting components on held-out data leaks its distribution into the pipeline.
Trade: Lower dimensions save work but may discard task-relevant information.
Try: Fit a projection on training data and inspect reconstruction and minority-class errors separately.
worked_case: A rare fraud signal can contribute little overall variance and disappear when only the largest components are retained. A high explained-variance percentage can therefore coexist with worse detection of the important minority case.

Q: How do conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule differ?
A: Conditional probability measures an event within a stated conditioning population. Independence means conditioning on one event does not change the probability of the other under the model; it is an assumption to justify, not a default property. Bayes' rule relates a reversed conditional through the prior and evidence probability. Confusing the probability of a positive test given disease with disease given a positive test ignores prevalence. Use a contingency table when denominators are easy to confuse, especially for rare-event classifiers.
Why: With 100 truly positive cases among 10,000, 90 detections and 99 false alerts produce precision 90/189 even though sensitivity is 90/100. The two probabilities answer different operational questions.
Risk: A changing deployment prevalence can change positive predictive value without changing sensitivity.
Trade: Tables clarify denominators; probability models generalize when assumptions are stated.
Try: Recalculate alert precision after reducing prevalence while keeping the test rates fixed.
worked_case: With 100 truly positive cases among 10,000, 90 detections and 99 false alerts produce precision 90/189 even though sensitivity is 90/100. The two probabilities answer different operational questions.

Q: How do expectation, variance and covariance describe uncertain quantities?
A: Expectation is a probability-weighted mean, variance measures squared deviation around that mean, and covariance captures how two quantities vary together. Covariance depends on scale; correlation normalizes it under nonzero finite variances. Zero correlation does not generally prove independence, and correlation does not establish causation. Distinguish variability among individual observations from uncertainty in an estimated mean. For operational data, dependent observations and changing conditions can invalidate simple independent-sample uncertainty calculations.
Why: Repeated requests from one customer can be strongly related. Treating each as an independent sample may make an estimate seem more precise than a customer-level analysis supports.
Risk: Averages can hide multimodal or high-tail behavior.
Trade: Summary statistics are useful when paired with distribution and sampling context.
Try: Compare per-request and per-customer summaries for a dataset with repeated customers.
worked_case: Repeated requests from one customer can be strongly related. Treating each as an independent sample may make an estimate seem more precise than a customer-level analysis supports.

Q: How do derivatives, partial derivatives and the chain rule produce gradients?
A: A derivative describes local sensitivity to one input. A partial derivative changes one coordinate while holding the others fixed, and a gradient collects those partial derivatives for a scalar objective. The chain rule propagates sensitivity through composed operations, which is the basis of backpropagation. A gradient is local information, not a guarantee that a large step improves the objective. Check shapes, nondifferentiable points and numerical scale, and compare a small analytic result with a finite-difference approximation where appropriate.
Why: For loss (w*x-y)^2, the derivative with respect to w is 2*(w*x-y)*x. With x=2, y=3 and w=1, the derivative is -4; a sufficiently small positive learning-rate update increases w.
Risk: Large finite-difference steps and floating-point cancellation can both mislead gradient checks.
Trade: Analytic or automatic derivatives scale; finite differences help validate small smooth cases.
Try: Derive one scalar gradient and compare it with a centered finite difference.
worked_case: For loss (w*x-y)^2, the derivative with respect to w is 2*(w*x-y)*x. With x=2, y=3 and w=1, the derivative is -4; a sufficiently small positive learning-rate update increases w.

Q: Why do conditioning, numerical stability and log-space calculations matter?
A: A well-defined formula can still be numerically fragile. Conditioning describes sensitivity of a problem's output to input changes, while numerical stability concerns how an algorithm amplifies finite-precision effects. Exponentiating large logits can overflow even though softmax probabilities are finite; subtracting the largest logit preserves the mathematical distribution while improving computation. Very small probabilities can underflow when multiplied, so log-space accumulation is often useful. State precision and tolerance instead of expecting every mathematically equivalent expression to compute identically.
Why: Softmax of logits 1000 and 1001 can overflow with direct exponentials. Subtracting 1001 yields logits -1 and 0 with the same probabilities and finite intermediate values.
Risk: Clipping every unusual value can conceal a faulty model or data pipeline.
Trade: Stable algorithms preserve intended calculations without claiming arbitrary precision.
Try: Compare naive and stabilized softmax on large logits and verify probabilities sum approximately to one.
worked_case: Softmax of logits 1000 and 1001 can overflow with direct exponentials. Subtracting 1001 yields logits -1 and 0 with the same probabilities and finite intermediate values.

Q: How do confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and effect sizes answer different questions?
A: A confidence interval describes an estimation procedure's repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions; it is not generally a probability that a fixed parameter lies in one observed interval. A hypothesis test evaluates data against a specified null model. Effect size describes the magnitude of a difference, which may matter more operationally than a small p-value. Account for paired observations, clustering, multiple comparisons and selection. Repeatedly checking and stopping when a result looks favorable can invalidate an ordinary fixed-sample interpretation.
Why: Two models evaluated on the same examples create paired outcomes. Comparing independent unpaired summaries throws away that structure, while searching dozens of models and reporting only the best can exaggerate improvement.
Risk: Statistical significance does not guarantee useful size or relevance to deployment.
Trade: Use a design matching the decision and report uncertainty with practical thresholds.
Try: Compare paired model errors and state a useful minimum improvement before inspecting the result.
worked_case: Two models evaluated on the same examples create paired outcomes. Comparing independent unpaired summaries throws away that structure, while searching dozens of models and reporting only the best can exaggerate improvement.
